deep.reconstruction:
Page 65 opens Chapter XIV of the Tractatus de numerorum doctrina: quadratic residues modulo composite numbers. It treats the modulus 2q, where q = 2p+1 is an odd prime, and counts only squares coprime to the modulus.

§502 (setup). Mod the prime q = 2p+1 the quadratic residues 1, α, β, γ, ... number p. Question: which residues arise mod 2q from squares a^2 with gcd(a, 2q) = 1, i.e. a odd and not divisible by q?

§503 (upper bound). The units below 2q number φ(2q) = 2p. Since a^2 ≡ (2q−a)^2 = (4p+2−a)^2 (mod 2q), the units pair off as {a, 2q−a}. So there are at most p distinct residues.

§504 (no further coincidences). Suppose a^2 ≡ b^2 (mod 2q) with a, b odd units.
- Then 2q divides (b−a)(b+a).
- Euler: one factor must carry the 2 and the other (or the same) the q. Since a and b are both odd, b−a and b+a are both even.
- So whichever factor q divides is divisible by 2q. Hence b ≡ ±a (mod 2q), i.e. b = a or b = 2q−a (the case b = a is implicit; this remark is mine).

§505 (count). Exactly p distinct residues 1, A, B, C, ... mod 2q, the same number as mod q. Products of two residues are residues.

§506 (non-residues). The remaining p units 𝔄, 𝔅, ℭ, ... are non-residues. The product of two non-residues is a residue. In modern terms (U(2q) ≅ U(q) is cyclic, so the squares form a subgroup of index 2) this is correct; Euler asserts it without separate proof on this page.

§507 (tables). Residues and non-residues for:
- q = 3, 6: residues 1; non-residues 2 resp. 5.
- q = 5, 10: residues 1,4 / 1,9; non-residues 2,3 / 3,7.
- q = 7, 14: residues 1,2,4 / 1,9,11; non-residues 3,5,6 / 3,5,13.
- q = 11, 22: residues 1,3,4,5,9 / 1,3,5,9,15; non-residues 2,6,7,8,10 / 7,13,17,19,21.
- q = 13, 26: residues 1,3,4,9,10,12 / 1,3,9,17,23,25; non-residues 2,5,6,7,8,11 / 5,7,11,15,19,21.
- q = 17, 34: residues 1,2,4,8,9,13,15,16 / 1,9,13,15,19,21,25,33; non-residues 3,5,6,7,10,11,12,14 / 3,5,7,11,23,27,29,31.

The tables already exhibit the rule proved on the next page (§§509–514): the residues mod 2q are the odd residues mod q kept as they are, and the even ones increased by q. Likewise for non-residues. This is the CRT bijection between U(q) and U(2q).

§508 sets up general notation: α, β, ... and 𝔞, 𝔟, ... mod q; A, B, ... and 𝔄, 𝔅, ... mod 2q.
errors: No mathematical errors. All 12 table columns check out when recomputed.
§504's phrasing 'alter factor per 2, alter per 2p+1' is slightly loose: one factor might carry both. The conclusion is right because both factors are even.
The trivial case b = a is not mentioned.
§506's claim that the product of two non-residues mod 2q is a residue is stated without proof here. It is true, and follows from the correspondence with residues mod q established afterwards.

results.what: For an odd prime q, the units mod 2q contain exactly (q−1)/2 quadratic residues, since a^2 ≡ b^2 (mod 2q) implies b ≡ ±a.
results.modern_name: Quadratic residues modulo 2p; index of squares in the cyclic group U(2p) ≅ U(p)
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore; systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), §§100–105 on residues to composite moduli

results.what: Residues and non-residues mod 2q are the odd representatives of those mod q (even ones increased by q). Exhibited in the tables; proved on the next page.
results.usually_credited_to: Classical; Gauss 1801 for the general treatment

results.what: Products of two residues, and of two non-residues, are residues mod 2q.
results.modern_name: Multiplicativity of the quadratic character on (Z/2qZ)^*

deep.surprise_reason: This is elementary, routine material from Euler's Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (c. 1750), published in the Opera postuma (1862). It is already known as his and is completely standard; the tables are correct.
